title: Focus a diode laser before cutting robot parts: carry its loosened module onto the focus bar, retighten, stow the bar
instruction: Focus the laser module on this plywood sheet before the robot-arm parts are cut. Turn the focus bar down. Hold the module so it cannot drop, loosen both hand screws, and lower the module until the hanging bar just touches the sheet. Tighten both hand screws, turn the bar back up onto its magnet, and let go of everything. Do not move the sheet.
context: Robot builders cut plate parts from 3 mm sheet on desktop laser cutters; the MeArm robot arm's parts fit on 300 x 200 mm of 3 mm sheet. The Creality CR-Laser Falcon 5W, an open-frame diode laser that cuts wood up to 5 mm thick, has no autofocus; Creality's guide sets the focus after each new material is placed: "the fixed focus bar should contact with the surface of the processed material when it is naturally vertical downward. Then lock it with two hand screws on the right and turn the fixed focus bar clockwise until it is attracted by the magnet." Only those screws hold the module, so with both loose it slides down its bracket. One hand carries it 12 mm down until the hanging bar just touches the sheet, never letting it fall, while the other turns the screws; it must stay within 0.5 mm of that contact as they are tightened. A robot that does this can run the machine that cuts its own parts.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases (61 cm apart at the table's near edge), x forward, y to the robot's left; heights above the table top. Nothing is random. Laser: a Creality CR-Laser Falcon 5W open-frame diode laser engraver (455 nm), unplugged, overall 568 x 632 x 198 mm, its front facing the robot. Its space-grey aluminium frame stands square on the table on corner feet: rails 4 cm wide, tops 4 cm up, outer edges at x 19 to 75.8 and y -31.6 to +31.6. Its grey gantry beam (4 x 3.3 cm, along y, 16.5 to 19.8 cm up, level with the module's top, front face at x 36) is pushed by hand so the laser module's axis is at (30, 5); the grey carriage plate and the fixing plate stand behind the module. Plate: 3 mm aluminium, 30 x 40 cm, taped flat on the table at x 24 to 54, y -15 to +25. Sheet: 3 mm basswood plywood, 20 x 30 cm, loose on the plate, long side along y, at x 25 to 45, y -10 to +20; tape marks on the plate at its two front corners. Laser module: black aluminium body 4.2 x 4.2 cm with its fan and driver board on top and, at its foot, a red transparent acrylic shield 5.0 cm wide, 4.6 cm deep and 4.2 cm tall; 12.6 cm from the shield's lower edge to the top; it slides vertically on the fixing plate. Two hand screws on its -y side, one above the other: silver knurled round heads 1.4 cm across and 0.8 cm thick on screws standing 0.5 cm off the side, axes along y, 1.8 cm in front of the module's back face, 5.9 and 8.9 cm above the shield's lower edge. Fixed focus bar on the same side, below them: a black T-shaped steel bar, its leg 7 mm wide and 2.5 mm thick with a rounded end, 3.9 cm from its pivot to its end; the pivot is 0.4 cm off the shield's side, 0.6 cm in front of the back face and 3.4 cm above the shield's lower edge. Hanging straight down, its end is 0.5 cm below the shield's lower edge; stowed, it is turned 90 degrees forward to level, its end toward the robot, on its magnet. Estimates: module 0.40 kg, bar 5 g, sheet 80 g, and the module's, screws' and bar's sizes above. Start: both screws light finger-tight (turned by thumb and finger until they stop, no more); the shield's lower edge 2.3 cm up, so the hanging bar's end would be 12 mm above the sheet; the bar stowed on its magnet. Both grippers open at the ready pose.
scoring: Real-trial tools: overhead and wrist video; a phone filming 240 fps slow motion on a small tripod 40 cm to the robot's left of the module, level with it and aimed at its +y face, with a 150 mm steel rule taped upright to the fixing plate beside that face and a pen line on tape across the face; a taper gap gauge (1 to 15 mm); a digital caliper; a pen and a printed protractor card; a ruler; tape marks. Focus error e: the hanging bar's end height above the sheet; real: the gap under the red shield's front lower edge (taper gauge) minus the hanging bar's reach below that edge (caliper); sim: the slide's position against the bar's contact position. In focus: e within 0.5 mm (the maker's set point, the hanging bar touching the material). Near focus: e within 2.0 mm. Locked: real, after e is read, each hand screw brought finger-tight by the judge's thumb and finger turns less than 30 degrees (pen line across its rim and the module); sim, both screws within 30 degrees of their snug stops. Bar stowed: on its magnet, within 10 degrees of its stowed angle. Released and still: both grippers (fingers and palm) 3 cm or more from the module (with its screws and bar) and from the sheet; the module, bar, screws and sheet each under 1 cm/s (sim: under 0.5 mm of movement in each 50 ms step). Latched 0 at any moment: (1) dropped: the module descends faster than 3 cm/s at any moment, touched or not (more than 1.5 mm within any 50 ms), or descends 2 mm or more while no gripper touches it (its body or either screw; the bar does not count), from its highest point since a gripper last touched it (real: the pen line against the rule on the 240 fps video, frame by frame; sim: the slide's descent over each 50 ms control step, and finger contacts every 240 Hz physics step); (2) moved: any sheet corner, or the module along either axis, more than 3 mm from its tape mark. The 3 cm/s line is this task's own: the module is carried down, never let fall; a steady, held lowering stays well under it, and a module falling freely passes it within its first 0.1 mm. The care itself is a maker's for the same step on its own open-frame laser (Snapmaker Ray wiki, adjusting the laser height): "before releasing the handle, make sure to hold the laser module securely to prevent it from slipping and falling, which may cause damage." Otherwise, at the end of the trial: 1.0: in focus, locked, bar stowed, released and still, held 1 s. 0.75: in focus, locked, released and still; bar not stowed, or the 1.0 state held under 1 s. 0.5: near focus but not in focus, locked, released and still. 0.25: in focus but not locked (one screw or neither at snug), released and still. 0: anything else, or any latch.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Hold the module, loosen both hand screws, and lower the module until the hanging bar rests on a 12 mm drill bit's shank lying on the sheet; turn both screws light finger-tight (thumb and finger until they stop, no more), take the shank away and turn the bar up onto its magnet. Put the sheet back on its tape marks, and the gantry so the module's tape marks line up. The machine stays unplugged throughout and the laser never fires; the module's cable stays plugged in, routed to the gantry as delivered. For every trial the gantry and the carriage stay where the setup puts them, held by small spring clamps: one on each side rail just in front of and one just behind the gantry's end plate, and one on the gantry beam each side of the carriage, all outside the work area. Cost: the CR-Laser Falcon 5W sells complete (frame, gantry, carriage, fixing plate, 5 W module with its focus bar, magnet and hand screws) for under US$200 (November 2026), for example from B&H Photo (Creality SKU 1005010023, bhphotovideo.com/c/product/1894685-REG) or Creality's own stores. Buy the 5W model: its focus bar is the hinged one on the module; the 10W model uses a loose stepped block instead. The aluminium plate and the plywood are ordinary stock. About 2 minutes per reset.
fidelity: Rigid bodies; frame, gantry and carriage fixed. Slide: prismatic joint, 5 N s/m damping (estimate). Hand screws: hinges, no thread, 0.15 N m finger-tight breakaway (estimate). A rule in task.py turns a screw only by a gripper's own turn about its axis while both pads press its head at 14 N or more, stopping at snug; a clamp rule holds the slide and carries the module while either screw is within 30 deg of snug. Magnet rule: 0.02 N m (estimate). Focus bar: a 2.5 mm strip with a 7 mm collider.
